In [[complex analysis]], a field in mathematics, the '''Remmert–Stein theorem''', introduced by {{harvs|txt | last1=Remmert | first1=Reinhold |author1-link=Reinhold Remmert| last2=Stein | first2=Karl |author2-link=Karl Stein (mathematician) | year=1953}}, gives conditions for the [[Closure (topology)|closure]] of an [[analytic variety|analytic set]] to be analytic.

The theorem states that if ''F'' is an analytic set of dimension less than ''k'' in some [[complex manifold]] ''D'', and ''M'' is an analytic subset of ''D''&nbsp;–&nbsp;''F'' with all components of dimension at least ''k'', then the closure of ''M'' is either analytic or contains ''F''.

The condition on the dimensions is necessary: for example, the set of points (1/''n'',0) in the [[complex plane]] is analytic in the complex plane minus the origin, but its closure in the complex plane is not.

==Relations to other theorems==

A consequence of the Remmert–Stein theorem (also treated in their paper), is [[Algebraic_geometry_and_analytic_geometry#Chow's_theorem|Chow's theorem]] stating that any projective complex [[analytic space]] is necessarily a [[projective algebraic variety]].

The Remmert–Stein theorem is implied by a [[Proper map|proper mapping theorem]] due to {{harvtxt|Bishop|1964}}, see {{harvtxt|Aguilar|Verjovsky|2021}}.
